Palm Fronds in Emirati Life

An illustrated timeline from oasis craft to contemporary souvenirs

A palm frond can become a food basket, a hand fan or a keepsake. This story follows the people who turn a familiar natural material into useful objects and Emirati art. Dates mark documented milestones; older crafts developed over generations rather than at one known moment.

1Roots in the Oasis

Centuries ago the date palm supplied the materialLearning to turn leaflets into khoosThe idea grew from everyday needs

Centuries ago the date palm supplied the material

The fronds come from the date palm, the tree that grows dates. A frond has narrow leaflets along a strong central rib. In UAE oasis communities, especially around Al Ain and Liwa, palms connected food, farming and making. Al Ain’s long agricultural history explains this setting; it does not give an exact invention date for weaving. [1, 2]

Learning to turn leaflets into khoos

Khoos, also written khous, names palm leaf material and the craft of weaving it. Makers select leaves, prepare and dry them, soften them in water, then weave or braid strips. The softer inner leaves suit finer work. Colour can be added before weaving. Simple tools, patient hands and an available local plant made the craft practical. [2]

The idea grew from everyday needs

People needed ways to carry a harvest, protect a meal and cool themselves. Making with nearby materials answered those needs. Both women and men practised khoos, and skills passed from one generation to another. Patterns and colour choices also gave each maker space for personal artistry. [3]

Read the photographs as living examples of the techniques. They are contemporary craft images, rather than historical photographs of the period described. Local object names and English spellings can vary.

2Everyday Uses Before Oil

Everyday life before the oil era

Before the 1960s sharing mealsCovering foodStoring and moving foodCooling people and shading the headCarrying the daily catch and market purchases

Before the 1960s sharing meals

The surood was a circular woven mat on which food was placed. It provided a dining surface for shared meals on the floor. This is the heritage link behind today’s palm inspired dining tables. [3]

Covering food

The makabah, also called a mekkab or majaba in different sources, covered and protected food. Its raised shape created space above the dish. The form survives in contemporary handmade homeware. [3, 16]

Storing and moving food

Zabil baskets came in different sizes for different jobs. They carried dates and grain, and some held household belongings. Palm containers were tailored to the task, rather than made in one standard shape. [4]

Cooling people and shading the head

The mahafah or hand fan moved air to cool a person and could also fan a flame. Palm leaf hats offered shade from the sun. Hats are documented among UAE khoos products; their forms belong to a wider Gulf tradition too. [3, 6, 7]

Carrying the daily catch and market purchases

The jafeer was a woven basket with handles. Coastal communities used it to carry fish; inland communities used it for dates and market purchases. Its carrying function helps explain the move towards today’s palm leaf bags. Jafeer baskets also continue in sweet giving at weddings and other occasions. [5]

For younger readers, connect each shape to its job. A broad mat holds a meal, a cone covers it, a fan moves air and handles make a basket portable.

3A New Role for an Inherited Skill

Late twentieth century to the 2010s

Modern life changed the demand2009 onwards from household craft to giftsThe 2010s onwards watch the skill being taught

Modern life changed the demand

As modern containers and household tools spread, some woven palm objects became less common in everyday use. The zabil increasingly became an object of heritage and memory. The knowledge remained valuable because families, makers and cultural institutions continued to share it. [4, 20]

2009 onwards from household craft to gifts

Khalifa Fund established Sougha in 2009 to revive Emirati heritage and help artisans turn their skills into careers. Its palm leaf beach bags show how a familiar material can meet a visitor’s present day needs. A souvenir now carries the maker’s skill as well as a memory of a place. [9, 10]

The 2010s onwards watch the skill being taught

At Abu Dhabi’s House of Artisans, demonstrations and workshops connect visitors with living craft. Meeting a maker makes the story easier to understand: the pattern comes from repeated actions, learned and practised over time. [20]

4Contemporary Design and Written Souvenirs

2019 to the present

2019 heritage gains international recognition2019 weaving becomes contemporary furnitureA written souvenir connects a person to the palmHow the keepsake revives Emirati art2024 farm material becomes handmade homeware2025 the dining mat inspires a dining tableToday new materials extend the craft2026 makers continue to demonstrate and adaptMake the story part of your own experience

2019 heritage gains international recognition

The UAE joined the multinational UNESCO inscription of date palm knowledge, skills, traditions and practices in 2019. An extended inscription followed in 2022. The heritage includes knowledge held by people, such as growing palms and making with their parts. [11, 12]

2019 weaving becomes contemporary furniture

Lana El Samman’s Mokaab developed from the idea of arish, traditional palm leaf architecture. It combines woven palm fronds and camel leather with oak and steel in units that work as tables or shelves. The innovation lies in adapting inherited weaving to a new structure and use. [13, 21]

2022 palm art and keepsakes

A written souvenir connects a person to the palm

Emirati artist Azza Al Qubaisi found inspiration in pruned palm material on her family’s Liwa farm in the early 2000s. At the 2022 Smithsonian Folklife Festival, visitors painted palm pieces to take home as magnets. The photographed examples include Arabic calligraphy. These pieces use kurub, the firm bases of palm leaves, rather than woven strips. [14]

How the keepsake revives Emirati art

A personalised name or message can add an individual memory to a local material. This is a contemporary interpretation of heritage: palm making meets lettering and painting. Al Qubaisi’s collaborative Palm Eye Flower shows the link between this material, artistic expression and shared participation. [15]

Written palm keepsakes connect to documented Emirati palm art. The sources do not establish one inventor or a start date for today’s wider souvenir trend.

2024 and 2025 new life in homes

2024 farm material becomes handmade homeware

In Fujairah, Mouza Yammahy’s Bint Aldar uses dried palm fronds for baskets, mats and food covers. A 2024 account describes her idea growing from seeing material discarded after a harvest. Familiar skills give that material another useful life. [16]

2025 the dining mat inspires a dining table

Tashkeel’s Khoos Dining Set reinterprets the circular dining mat and its tradition of gathering. The tabletop echoes interlaced palm patterns. The catalogue identifies ash wood with metallic gold paint: this table carries the visual language of khoos, rather than being a table made entirely from palm fronds. [17]

A table can incorporate actual woven palm material, as Mokaab does, or translate its pattern into another material. Both routes connect modern design to the older dining story. [13, 17]

2026 keeping the story in use

Today new materials extend the craft

The Nakhla Stool Series combines a palm leaf mat, handwoven by Mariam Al Dhaheri, with DesertBoard made from waste palm fronds. Two stacked units become a standing table. It shows how handmade weaving and new material processing can work together. [18]

2026 makers continue to demonstrate and adapt

At Sharjah Heritage Days in February 2026, Abdullah Ali Ahmed Al Shuhhi demonstrated jirban, palm containers for storing dates. Maryam Ali Rashid’s handmade palm frond bags were also displayed. The craft continues through work, teaching and new products. [19]

Make the story part of your own experience

UAE families can record a relative’s explanation of a basket or fan. Tourists can meet an artisan and ask about the palm material before choosing a keepsake. Generation Alpha can trace a woven pattern, try supervised weaving or paint a prepared palm piece. These are ways to turn looking into learning.

When a written souvenir preserves the material’s story, acknowledges the maker and brings someone into contact with the craft, it can help heritage remain part of contemporary Emirati life. The palm object becomes a reminder of the land, the skill and the person who made it. [15, 20]

Glossary

Simple meanings of the craft words used in this story.

Date palm

The tree that grows dates. A frond has narrow leaflets along a strong central rib.

Khoosalso written khous

Palm leaf material and the craft of weaving it.

Surood

A circular woven mat on which food was placed. It was a dining surface for shared meals on the floor.

Makabahalso called mekkab or majaba

A raised cover that protected food and created space above the dish.

Zabil

Baskets in different sizes for different jobs. They carried dates and grain, and some held household belongings.

Mahafah

A hand fan. It moved air to cool a person and could also fan a flame.

Jafeeralso written jefeer

A woven basket with handles. Coastal communities carried fish in it; inland communities used it for dates and market purchases.

Jirban

Palm containers for storing dates.

Kurub

The firm bases of palm leaves.

Arish

Traditional palm leaf architecture.
